title: Kapila Charitram
body:
Kapila Charitram

Kapila was no ordinary child, for He was Bhagavan Himself, descending into the world to reveal the highest knowledge and to guide those who sought liberation. His father was Kardama Muni, a great sage who had spent countless years in deep penance in solitude. Pleased with his devotion, Sriman Narayana appeared before him and granted him a rare boon — that the Lord Himself would be born as his son.
Kardama, however, had another duty to fulfill first. Swayambhuva Manu, the ruler of the world and son of Brahma, approached him seeking a suitable groom for his daughter Devahuti — a princess of great beauty, humility, and devotion. Though Kardama had lived detached from worldly affairs, he accepted the proposal, understanding it to be part of a greater design, and assured Devahuti that once his duties as a householder were complete he would renounce the world, and that she too should prepare herself for the path of liberation. It is said that when the Lord had descended to grant this boon, He arrived seated upon Garuda, and as Garuda beat his wings the sound of the Sama Veda mantras was heard — a sign that the essence of the Vedas rests upon the Vedas themselves, and that the Lord who rides upon them is the Purushottama celebrated in the Upanishads.
For years Devahuti served her husband with unwavering devotion, embracing the austere life of an ascetic's wife though she had once known only royal comfort. In time nine daughters were born to them, and then a son — Kapila, the Supreme Lord in human form. Even as a child His presence filled the hermitage with an indescribable peace, His lotuslike eyes shining with the brilliance of eternity. His duties as a householder now complete, Kardama bowed before his own divine son, sought his blessings, and departed for the forests to spend his remaining years in meditation.
Devahuti, left in the presence of her divine child, had one final request. She turned to Kapila not as a mother to her son but as a seeker to her teacher, and asked how one might gain mastery over the senses and be freed from the endless cycle of birth and death. In answer, Kapila revealed to her the knowledge of Sankhya — the eternal truth of the soul and the path to liberation. He taught that this body and this world are but a play of prakriti, material nature, formed from twenty-four elements: the five great elements, the five senses, the mind, intelligence, ego, and the unmanifest material energy. The soul, the twenty-fifth principle, stands distinct from all of these; it is bound only by its false identification with the body, and the one who truly understands this is no longer moved by joy or sorrow, gain or loss.
Devahuti then asked how the soul comes to take shape within a mortal body, and Kapila explained to her the making of a human life. He described how the fertilized seed forms into a small mass within ten days; how the head takes shape by the end of the first month and the limbs by the second; how the nails, hair, skin, and organs form by the third month, and the blood, flesh, fat, bones, marrow, and vital fluids by the fourth. By the fifth month the child feels hunger and thirst; by the sixth it settles within the enveloping membrane and, tasting the food the mother eats, begins to develop taste. By the seventh month it turns its head downward and, feeling the confinement of the space, becomes aware of the sounds around it. In the eighth month, it is said, the child remembers all its previous births and even catches a glimpse of the Lord, and is filled with joy. By the ninth month it is ready to be born, delivered head first, its head still soft. And as it emerges into the air, a certain force acts upon it and causes it to forget all that it once knew of its former lives, so that the newborn cries in sorrow at all it has lost.
Kapila counseled his mother to place her whole faith in Sriman Narayana, for devotion alone is the path to liberation — the one who chants His name with love and serves Him without expectation is already free, even while living in this world. As Devahuti absorbed this wisdom her mind grew free of ignorance; she saw herself no longer as queen, wife, or mother, but only as the soul, and in time she attained liberation, her being merging into the divine. Kapila, having fulfilled His purpose, left the hermitage and traveled across the lands, sharing the knowledge of Sankhya and devotion for the awakening of countless souls.
